messages:
maya: quick question — I'm wiring up a pod (IRSA) in account-A to decrypt secrets with a KMS key that lives in shared-services account-B. I tried creating an aws_kms_grant in account-B via Terraform but the pod still gets AccessDenied. Do I need a provider alias / assume_role for the tf resource or am I missing a key policy change?

samir: you need both pieces usually. Grants can work cross-account if you create the grant in the key account with the grantee principal set to the role ARN from account-A (the IRSA role). But the key policy must allow the principal to use the key (or allow kms:CreateGrant + kms:Decrypt depending on flow).

elaine: fwiw we generally prefer a minimal key policy that allows the account root and a dedicated identity to manage grants, then create explicit grants for cross-account roles. grants are easier to revoke without changing the key policy.

maya: here's my tf snippet — is my provider usage wrong?
```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-west-2"
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "shared"
  region = "us-west-2"
  assume_role {
    role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::222222222222:role/terraform-key-admin"
  }
}

resource "aws_kms_grant" "irsa_pod" {
  provider = aws.shared
  name    = "irsa-pod-grant"
  key_id  = aws_kms_key.shared_key.key_id
  grantee_principal = "arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/eks-irsa-role"
  operations = ["Decrypt", "GenerateDataKey"]
}
```

maya: plan succeeded but pod still 403 when decrypting.

tyler: quick checks: 1) validate the grantee_principal matches the exact role ARN used by IRSA (double-check namespace suffix), 2) confirm the pod actually assumes that role (aws sts get-caller-identity from inside pod), 3) check key policy — if it explicitly denies or doesn't allow kms:CreateGrant for the principal that created the grant, it can block.

samir: also: when creating grants via TF in account-B you must use credentials that have kms:CreateGrant on the key. That means your provider alias approach is correct (assume terraform-key-admin in account-B). Without assume_role the create will attempt against the wrong account.

maya: ran `kubectl exec -it pod -- aws sts get-caller-identity --region us-west-2` and it returned the IRSA role ARN so pod is assuming right role.

elaine: next thing: check the grant's constraints. If you added an encryption_context_equals in the grant but your encrypt/decrypt calls don't set that exact context, Decrypt will fail. Also note some SDK callers don't set encryption context by default.

maya: I didn't set encryption_context. grant shows operations Decrypt + GenerateDataKey. key policy currently: grants ManageKey to account root + Admin role, no explicit cross-account principal. Could that be blocking usage?

samir: not directly — if the grant was created and active, it should allow the grantee_principal to use the key even without key policy change. But some KMS APIs check key policy too. safest path: add a principal statement in key policy allowing the IRSA role to use Decrypt and GenerateDataKey (or allow the account that manages grants to CreateGrant and Delegate). Example minimal statement: 
```json
{
  "Sid": "AllowIRSAUse",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/eks-irsa-role"},
  "Action": ["kms:Decrypt","kms:GenerateDataKey"],
  "Resource": "*"
}
```

tyler: also check CloudTrail for KMS:Decrypt failures — it will show whether the denial came from key policy or IAM. There was a gotcha where cross-account role ARNs need the full path, not partial.

maya: Changed key policy to include that AllowIRSAUse statement and recreated the grant (deleted and re-created with terraform apply using aws.shared). Still 403. CloudTrail shows KMS:Decrypt denied due to "not authorized by resource policy".

samir: ok that means key policy didn't match what KMS expected. Confirm that the ARN used in the policy exactly matches the principal from sts call (no session suffix). For IRSA the assumed role session principal may be `arn:aws:sts::111111111111:assumed-role/eks-irsa-role/sa-namespace-sa-name` but KMS expects the role ARN `arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/eks-irsa-role` in the policy. You're using role ARN so that should be fine.

elaine: another edge: if the key has a grant_token being used (rare) or if the SDK uses the issuer for temporary creds, verify the pod's request isn't using a different region or key alias. e.g., using alias/my-key vs actual key_id with different account.

maya: I noticed the pod is calling KMS via ciphertext that references alias/our-app-key — alias is in account-B (shared). Using key_id vs alias didn't change result.

samir: Last thing I can think: if the key's policy has a condition limiting principals to the same AWS account or requiring aws:PrincipalOrgID, cross-account role might be blocked. Share your key policy JSON?

maya: pasted key policy snippet:
```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {"Sid":"EnableIAMAdmin","Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::222222222222:role/terraform-key-admin"},"Action":"kms:*","Resource":"*"},
    {"Sid":"RootAccess","Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::222222222222:root"},"Action":"kms:*","Resource":"*"}
  ]
}
```

maya: so I added the AllowIRSAUse statement as you suggested but result same.

tyler: if the key policy is very restrictive (only allows account-B principals) it will block. You need either to allow the IRSA role ARN, or have the account-B admin principal allowed to CreateGrant and that grant explicitly names the role ARN. Since you created the grant from account-B, ensure that terraform-key-admin principal is the one creating the grant; CloudTrail should show CreateGrant success. Do you see a CreateGrant event?

maya: CloudTrail shows CreateGrant succeeded just before the Decrypt attempts. CreateGrant principal is terraform-key-admin. Grant ARN looks valid and shows grantee_principal = arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/eks-irsa-role.

samir: hmm. If CreateGrant succeeded but Decrypt still fails citing key policy, then KMS is evaluating the key policy before grants. KMS docs: key policy plus grants both apply; but some requests require key policy to allow the requestor or allow the caller to use grants. Recommendation: add a statement in key policy allowing `kms:Decrypt` for the principal `arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/eks-irsa-role` (explicit allow). After that, try again.

maya: did that, then redeployed pod. Still 403.

elaine: are you using SDK v3? there was a bug with certain versions and cross-account grants that used a weird principal mapping. What does the client call look like?

maya: using aws-sdk-go v2 via our internal secrets library, calling `Decrypt` with ciphertext only. No encryption context.

samir: last debugging step: run an aws-cli decrypt from an EC2 instance in account-A that has the same role, see if that works. If it does, issue is likely in pod environment/credentials. If it fails, it's definitely KMS policy.

maya: good point — I'll spin up a small ec2 with the role attached and test. will report back. thanks all. :thumbsup:

infra-ci: plan: terraform apply —target=aws_kms_grant.irsa_pod in aws.shared completed in 23s. No drift detected.

(2 hours later) maya: update — ran ec2 test with same role, `aws kms decrypt` works from EC2 in account-A. So the grant + key policy are correct. Pod still 403. Suspect IRSA token or kube-proxy env. investigating networking to STS endpoints and kube IAM webhook.

samir: good isolate. if EC2 works but pod doesn't, it's kube auth to STS. check the OIDC issuer thumbprint and service account annotation sti/corrupted? Also inspect `kubectl -n ns get sa sa-name -o yaml` to confirm annotation `eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/eks-irsa-role` is present.

maya: found it — our service account annotation was pointing to an outdated role arn (typo in account ID). Fixing now and redeploying. Should have been a simple string error :grimacing:

tyler: classic. glad the TF bits were mostly right. Good checklist to keep: 1) provider alias + assume_role for key-account TF, 2) create grant with grantee = role ARN, 3) ensure key policy allows either the role or the grant-creator to CreateGrant, 4) verify pod actually assumes the role.

maya: confirmed — after fixing annotation pod decrypts fine. thanks everyone for the pointers. saved me a lot of hair. :sparkles:
